title: Mahinda to Sri Lanka
hookLine: Ashoka's son Mahinda brings the teaching to the island (Mahavamsa 14)

cards: A king is hunting on a mountain, chasing a deer through the trees, bow in hand, his men somewhere behind him. Then a voice calls him by name.

He turns, and on the rock above him stands a monk in robes, calm, unarmed, waiting. The king is Devanampiya Tissa, ruler of the island of Lanka. The monk, the Mahavamsa says, is Mahinda, son of the emperor Ashoka.
The deer is gone. The conversation is about to begin.

teach.b: First, the test. Before he teaches anything, Mahinda checks whether the king can think. He points to a tree.
What is this called? A mango. Are there other mangoes besides this one?
Many. And besides this mango and the other mangoes, are there other trees? Many, but they aren't mangoes.
And besides the other mangoes and the trees that aren't mangoes, is there another? Yes, says the king: this mango tree.
Then the same about relatives, and the king answers: besides my kin and those who aren't my kin, there's myself. The chronicle says Mahinda saw the king was sharp, and ready.
Mahinda preaches a discourse there on the mountain, and the king takes refuge with the people around him. Third, a son of an emperor.
In the chronicle, Mahinda had left a prince's life to become a monk, and was sent out after the council at Pataliputta. Tradition says Ashoka's own children carried the teaching to the island.

teach.h: THIS WEEK: FROM SPLIT TO SEA.
teach.b: However historians weigh the chronicle, in its telling this meeting is where the island's Buddhist story begins. Fourth, the week behind us. A split, the Sthaviras and the Mahasanghikas, and accounts that differ.
Eighteen schools and many readings. Ashoka's remorse, carved in stone. His edicts asking respect for every faith.
Wells, medicine and shade. A council the chronicles remember. And now a monk on a rock, and a teaching that has crossed the sea.

how: Sri Lankan Buddhists remember Mahinda's arrival each year at the Poson full moon, when pilgrims climb the hill of Mihintale, where tradition places the meeting with the king.

the king of Lanka who went out hunting a deer

games.q: the teaching crossed the sea: tap the pairs.

s: Mahinda began by preaching a long sermon
he began with a riddle about a mango tree, to see whether the king could think.
the king was hunting when he met Mahinda
in the Mahavamsa he's chasing a deer on a mountain when a voice calls his name.

games.q: you're a monk sent to teach a king you've never met. he's out hunting, bow in hand. how do you start?
o: a long sermon on the spot.
a simple riddle, to see how he thinks.
wait for him to come to you.
games.why: Mahinda asks about a mango tree: other mangoes, other trees, and what's left. the king answers well, and the teaching begins.

practice: Think back to how whatever you hold most deeply first reached you, a faith, a practice, a way of being kind, a love of quiet, and let one face come to mind: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, a stranger, a book someone left lying around.
Hold them with gratitude for a few breaths, whether they're near, far, or gone.

wordCard.voice: Mahinda. Ashoka's son, who met the island's king on a mountain and tested him with a riddle about a mango tree.

carryVoice: Your line: the teaching crossed the sea. In the chronicle, it arrived with a riddle on a hunting trip. Day eight hundred sixty-one, and a week complete.
